title: Why is single-threaded Redis so fast

segments.text: Why is Reddit so fast?
What fundamental design decisions did the developers make more than a decade ago?
That's true to test of time.
Let's take a look.
Red is a very popular in memory database.
It's rock solid, easy to use, and fast.
These attributes explain why it is one of the most loved databases, according to the
Stack Overflows Annual Developer Survey.
The first reason Red is fast is because it is an in memory database.
Memory access is several orders of magnitude faster than random this I.O.
Pure memory access provides high read and write throughput and low latency.
The trade-off is that the data set cannot be larger than memory.
Co-wise, in memory data structures are also much easier to implement than on this counterparts.
This keeps the code simple, and it contributes to Red's rock solid stability.
Another reason Red is fast is a bit unintuitive.
It is primarily single threaded.
Why would a single threaded design lead to high performance?
Wouldn't it be faster if it uses thread to leverage all the CPU course?
A multi-threaded applications require locks or other synchronization mechanisms.
There are notoriously a hard to reason about.
In many applications, the added complexity is bug-prong and sacrifices stability.
Making it difficult to justify the performance gain.
In the case of Reds, the single threaded code path is easy to understand.
How does the single threaded code base handle many thousands of incoming requests and outgoing responses at the same time?
Wouldn't the thread get blocked, rating for the completion of each request individually?
Now, this is where I.O. multiplexing comes into the picture.
With I.O. multiplexing, the operating system allows a single thread to weigh a many socket connections simultaneously.
Traditionally, this is done with the select or pull system course.
These system course are not very performant when there are many thousands of connections.
On Linux, E-Pull is a performance variant of I.O. multiplexing that supports many many thousands of connections in constant time.
A drawback of this single threaded design is that it does not leverage all the CPU cores available in modern hardware.
For some workloads, it is not uncommon to have several reds instances running on a single server to utilize more CPU cores.
We alluded to the third reason why Reds is fast.
Since Reds is an in-memory database, it could leverage several efficient low-level data structures,
without worrying about how to persist them to this efficiently.
Linkless, skipless, and hash table are some examples.
It is true that there are attempts at implementing new Reds compatible servers
to squeeze more performance of a single server.
With Reds' ease of use, rock solid stability and performance,
it is in our view that Reds still provides the best performance and stability trade-off in the market.
